ApostropheCMS SSPP __proto__ PATCH payload via $pullAll (CVE-2026-53609) AIExploitation High
Hunts the exploitation request for CVE-2026-53609: an authenticated-editor PATCH to a piece-type doc endpoint whose body carries a prototype-pollution path (e.g. $pullAll:{"__proto__.publicApiProjection":[]}). Article-specific because it keys on the literal __proto__/constructor/prototype/$pullAll tokens against the ApostropheCMS /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* PATCH surface, not a generic web attack. Rationale: Keys on the exact exploitation primitive from the PoC (Step 3): a PATCH to /api/v1/@apostrophecms/<piece> whose $pullAll body contains __proto__.publicApiProjection. __proto__/constructor/prototype tokens in a CMS PATCH are near-zero in benign editor traffic. Cross-checked against the GitLab advisory mirror and ApostropheCMS piece REST-API docs. Defender/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: this is inbound server-side web/WAF telemetry that XDR/FDR/CloudTrail do not carry. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/apostrophecms-critical-prototype-pollution-leads-to-auth-bypass/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test or bug-bounty submission replaying the CVE-2026-53609 PoC
  • Automated web vulnerability scanner (Burp/Nuclei) firing prototype-pollution templates at the CMS
  • Developer QA against a staging Apostrophe instance
  • A field legitimately named with a double-underscore prefix in a custom schema (rare)
  • WAF appliance that URL-decodes and reflects the full body into RequestContext creating duplicate log lines
Suppression filter
| where RequestURL !has "/staging/"  // add: and SourceIP !in (<authorized-scanner-CIDR-list>) once your scanner egress ranges are known
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the request was a PATCH to a /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* doc endpoint returning HTTP 200 and that the body/context contains __proto__ (not just the word in a legit field). Identify the SourceIP and the editor account/bearer token used. 2) CONTAIN: Restart the affected Node.js process immediately (pollution persists in memory until restart) and upgrade Apostrophe to 4.31.0+. Revoke/rotate the editor credential that sent the PATCH and force re-auth. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the SourceIP and server host for subsequent unauthenticated 200 responses on /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user and /global (UC: authorization-bypass outcome), and review who else authenticated as that editor.
// WAF/reverse-proxy with request-body inspection required (the __proto__ payload is in the JSON body, not the URI)
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/" and RequestURL has "@apostrophecms"
| where RequestURL has_any ("__proto__", "constructor", "prototype")
    or RequestContext has_any ("__proto__", "constructor", "prototype", "pullAll")
    or Message has_any ("__proto__", "constructor", "prototype", "pullAll")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestContext, Message, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

ApostropheCMS auth-bypass outcome: unauthenticated 200 on protected piece-type endpoints (CVE-2026-53609) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the process-wide authorization bypass state after CVE-2026-53609 pollution: GET requests to normally-protected piece-type REST endpoints (@apostrophecms/user, @apostrophecms/global) returning HTTP 200 with no session cookie / Authorization header. Pre-exploit these return notfound; a 200 to an unauthenticated /user listing is the bypass fingerprint. Rationale: Article verifies /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user and /global flip from notfound (Step 1) to a 200 paginated body (Step 4) with no credentials. A 200 on an anonymous GET of the user-listing endpoint is inherently anomalous per ApostropheCMS docs (these require auth unless publicApiProjection is set, which /user and /global are not). Confirmed against the ApostropheCMS piece REST-API reference and the GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://apostrophecms.com/docs/reference/api/pieces.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1548 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A piece type deliberately configured with publicApiProjection so anonymous GET is expected (exclude those specific piece names, but keep @apostrophecms/user and /global in scope)
  • Authenticated admin/API integration whose bearer token or session cookie the log pipeline failed to parse
  • Uptime/health-check monitor hitting the endpoint (whitelist its source IP)
  • Search-engine or archival crawler indexing an intentionally-public API
  • CDN/edge cache serving a previously-cached 200 body
Suppression filter
| where not (Url has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/@public-piece-name")  // exclude piece types intentionally exposed via publicApiProjection; keep user/global in scope
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Verify the endpoint is /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user or /global (should never be public) and confirm the request carried no Authorization header / apos session cookie yet returned 200. Check whether a UC1 __proto__ PATCH preceded it on the same host. 2) CONTAIN: Restart the Node.js process to clear the polluted Object.prototype and patch to Apostrophe 4.31.0+; block the exploiting source IP at the WAF. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all unauthenticated 200s across every /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* piece endpoint since the first hit to scope data exposure, and pull the editor login that seeded the pollution.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| where Url has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user" or Url has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global"
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) == 200
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderCookie) or HttpRequestHeaderCookie !has "apos"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpHostName, DstIpAddr
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

ApostropheCMS CVE-2026-53609 kill-chain: __proto__ PATCH followed by unauthenticated 200 bypass AIExploitation High
Correlates the two-step CVE-2026-53609 exploit within one source IP: a PATCH containing __proto__/$pullAll to an @apostrophecms endpoint, followed within 30 minutes by a successful (200) unauthenticated GET to /user or /global that was previously auth-gated. The sequence is far higher-confidence than either event alone. Rationale: Implements reviewer suggestion #4: the PoC walks PATCH ($pullAll __proto__, Step 3) then an unauthenticated 200 GET on /user (Step 4). Chaining both on one source IP within 30 minutes removes the residual FP of either half and directly evidences successful exploitation. Grounded in the GHSA PoC steps and corroborated by the GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1190 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentest replaying the full PoC from one workstation IP
  • A DAST scanner that both sends pollution payloads and then re-requests endpoints from the same egress IP
  • Shared corporate NAT/egress IP where one editor legitimately edits a doc and, coincidentally, a public-projection GET succeeds from the same IP within the window (mitigated by requiring the __proto__ token)
  • Load balancer collapsing client IPs so unrelated requests share a source IP
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm both legs share the source IP and target host and the delay is plausible (seconds-to-minutes); verify the PATCH body genuinely contained __proto__/$pullAll. This pairing is effectively a true positive. 2) CONTAIN: Restart the Node.js process to clear in-memory pollution, upgrade to Apostrophe 4.31.0+, block the source IP, and revoke the editor credential used for the PATCH. 3) HUNT: Determine the exposure window between pollution and process restart; enumerate every anonymous 200 across all piece endpoints during that window and treat any returned user/global data as disclosed.
let win = 30m;
let polluters = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where HttpMethod =~ "PATCH"
    | where Url has "@apostrophecms"
    | where Url has_any ("__proto__", "constructor", "prototype") or UrlOriginal has_any ("__proto__", "pullAll")
    | project PatchTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, PatchUrl = Url;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| where Url has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user" or Url has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global"
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) == 200
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| join kind=inner polluters on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (PatchTime .. PatchTime + win)
| project PatchTime, BypassTime = TimeGenerated, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, PatchTime), SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, PatchUrl, BypassUrl = Url
| sort by BypassTime desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t min(_time) as patch_time from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=PATCH Web.url="*@apostrophecms*" (Web.url="*__proto__*" OR Web.uri_query="*__proto__*" OR Web.uri_query="*pullAll*") by Web.src Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| rename src as attacker_src dest as target_host
| join type=inner attacker_src target_host [
    | tstats summariesonly=t min(_time) as bypass_time from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET (Web.url="*/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global*") Web.status=200 by Web.src Web.dest
    | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
    | rename src as attacker_src dest as target_host ]
| eval delay_sec = bypass_time - patch_time
| where delay_sec >= 0 AND delay_sec <= 1800
| convert ctime(patch_time) ctime(bypass_time)
| table attacker_src target_host patch_time bypass_time delay_sec
| sort - bypass_time
| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as patch_time from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=PATCH Web.url="*@apostrophecms*" (Web.url="*__proto__*" OR Web.uri_query="*__proto__*" OR Web.uri_query="*pullAll*") by Web.src Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`

    | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
    | rename src as attacker_src dest as target_host ]
| eval delay_sec = bypass_time - patch_time
| where delay_sec >= 0 AND delay_sec <= 1800
| convert ctime(patch_time) ctime(bypass_time)
| table attacker_src target_host patch_time bypass_time delay_sec
| sort - bypass_time
Attack-surface hunt: internet-exposed ApostropheCMS piece-type REST endpoints (CVE-2026-53609) AIReconnaissance Medium
Inventory hunt surfacing hosts serving the ApostropheCMS /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* REST API so responders can prioritise patching to 4.31.0 for CVE-2026-53609. Groups web traffic by destination host to reveal every Apostrophe instance and how many distinct clients probe it. Rationale: Implements reviewer suggestion #5. The /api/v1/@apostrophecms/ path prefix is a reliable ApostropheCMS fingerprint (confirmed in the product REST-API docs); grouping by destination host inventories exposed instances to scope CVE-2026-53609 (vuln <= 4.30.0, fixed 4.31.0). Marked hunting/high-FP because it surfaces all Apostrophe traffic, not malicious traffic alone. Cross-checked against: • https://apostrophecms.com/docs/reference/api/pieces.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1592.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate day-to-day CMS usage and authenticated editor/API traffic (expected, not malicious)
  • Internal monitoring/uptime checks hitting the API
  • Search-engine and archival crawlers
  • Front-door CDN aggregating many client IPs into few sources, understating unique_clients
  • Non-vulnerable but already-patched 4.31.0+ instances still matching the path fingerprint
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each surfaced HttpHostName/DstIpAddr, confirm it is an Apostrophe deployment and identify its version (banner, package manifest, or admin). 2) CONTAIN: Prioritise any instance <= 4.30.0 for upgrade to 4.31.0+; where immediate patching is impossible, restrict the /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* piece endpoints at the WAF and audit editor accounts (any editor can trigger the CVE). 3) HUNT: On each confirmed-vulnerable host, run the UC1 (__proto__ PATCH) and UC2 (unauthenticated 200) detections retroactively to check for prior exploitation.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
| summarize Requests = count(), UniqueClients = dcount(SrcIpAddr), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 10) by HttpHostName, DstIpAddr
| sort by Requests desc

Detected
Phase 6
Command & Control
Detected
Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Atomic Arch AUR loader/stealer known-bad file & process hashes · [LLM] Non-package-manager process writing systemd unit or cron persistence (Atomic Arch) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Tor client masquerading as dbus-daemon making external network connections · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SSH worm: persistence-path binary spawning ssh/scp for self-propagation · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Atomic Arch AUR loader/stealer known-bad file & process hashes AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution or on-disk presence of the July 2026 AUR (openconnect-sso) two-stage loader and Rust infostealer by their published SHA256/MD5 hashes. Article-specific: these hashes belong to the IFIN-analyzed Atomic Arch campaign redistributed through hijacked AUR package adoptions. Rationale: Uses the four campaign SHA256 hashes plus the MD5 pre-extracted from the article; SHA256 6144d433... is independently confirmed as the Rust stealer binary by The Hacker News and GuardSix, so hash-based matching is high-fidelity with near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse • https://discourse.ifin.network/t/new-aur-attack-prompts-adoption-lock/698
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in an authorized sandbox that reports to production EDR
  • Threat-intel/VirusTotal retrohunt downloads of the sample onto a research host
  • Incident-response tooling copying the artifact for evidence collection
  • Backup/AV quarantine re-scanning a previously captured copy
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("clamscan","freshclam","vt","virustotal") and FolderPath !has "/quarantine/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is Arch/Arch-based and whether any AUR package (openconnect-sso, boringssl-git, icloudpd, windscribe-cli-v2-bin, stirling-pdf-desktop-bin, pgadmin4-server) was recently installed/updated via makepkg. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the matching PID, and treat all local secrets (SSH keys, browser creds, cloud/dev/AI tokens) as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process, systemd units with Restart=always, and cron entries; rotate SSH keys and check known_hosts targets for lateral spread.

Tor client masquerading as dbus-daemon making external network connections AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Atomic Arch first-stage behaviour of launching a Tor client renamed to 'dbus-daemon' to reach an .onion C2. A legitimate dbus-daemon is a local IPC bus and never initiates public/internet egress, so any outbound public connection from a dbus-daemon process is high-fidelity. Rationale: Article states the loader 'downloads and launches a Tor client disguised as dbus-daemon' to reach an .onion server; corroborated by GuardSix noting C2 via a Tor onion service. dbus-daemon making public egress (Defender/Falcon) or running outside /usr/bin (Sentinel/Datadog/Sigma) is essentially never legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1036.005 T1573.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom-built dbus deployed to a non-standard prefix (/usr/local/bin) on developer boxes — path variant only
  • D-Bus remote/TCP transport intentionally configured in a container or CI runner
  • Chaos/network-testing tooling renamed to system binaries during red-team exercises
  • Flatpak/snap sandboxes shipping their own dbus-daemon under /app or /snap paths
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !in~ ("/usr/bin","/usr/local/bin") or RemotePort in (9001, 9030, 9050, 443)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full path, hash, and command line of the dbus-daemon process; a real one lives at /usr/bin/dbus-daemon and only talks to unix sockets — confirm the destination IP/port and whether it looks like a Tor guard node (443/9001). 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill the process; block the destination IP at egress. 3) Hunt: locate the parent AUR build (makepkg), the second-stage stealer under /var/lib or ~/.config, and any systemd/cron persistence; rotate all secrets on the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "dbus-daemon"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 10), RemoteIPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 25) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "dbus-daemon"
| where TargetProcessName !has "/usr/bin/dbus-daemon"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-package-manager process writing systemd unit or cron persistence (Atomic Arch) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the loader's persistence step: writing a systemd service (Restart=always) to /etc/systemd/system or ~/.config/systemd/user, plus cron jobs, from a process that is NOT a package manager or systemctl. Article-specific to the AUR loader installing systemd services and cron jobs after anti-analysis checks. Rationale: Article states the loader 'installs systemd services and cron jobs to ensure persistence'; StepSecurity/GuardSix confirm a Restart=always unit dropped to /etc/systemd/system (root) or ~/.config/systemd/user (user). Keying on non-package-manager writers to these exact paths captures the malicious writer while excluding legit installs to /usr/lib/systemd/system. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/400-aur-packages-hijacked-atomic-arch-campaign • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin hand-authoring a unit with a text editor (vim/nano) or writing crontab via a script
  • Configuration management (Ansible/Chef/Puppet/Salt) deploying systemd units or cron jobs
  • Developer enabling a user service under ~/.config/systemd/user for a legitimate app
  • Container build steps or dotfile-management tools writing unit files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","ansible-playbook","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion","vim","nano","vi","tee") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","puppet","chef","salt"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped unit/cron file — malicious ones point ExecStart at a binary under /var/lib, ~/.config, /tmp or /dev/shm and use Restart=always; benign ones point at packaged binaries in /usr/bin. 2) Contain: disable/remove the unit or cron entry, kill the referenced binary, and isolate the host if the target is a non-package path. 3) Hunt: pivot to the writing process's ancestry (makepkg build?), check for the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process and stealer artifacts, and rotate host secrets.

| where FileName endswith ".service" or FolderPath has "cron"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("systemctl","systemd","pacman","dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","dnf","yum","install","crontab")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

SSH worm: persistence-path binary spawning ssh/scp for self-propagation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Atomic Arch stealer's SSH worm capability — a binary running from a malware persistence directory (/var/lib, ~/.config, /tmp, /dev/shm) spawning ssh/scp/sftp/rsync to copy and execute itself on other hosts using stolen SSH keys. Distinguishes malware-driven lateral movement from interactive/administrative SSH. Rationale: Article states the stealer 'can spread laterally by using stolen SSH keys to copy and execute itself on other systems'; corroborated by StepSecurity/HackerNews noting SSH-key and known_hosts theft. Anchoring on ssh/scp spawned by a parent living in the confirmed persistence directories (/var/lib for root, ~/.config for user) targets the worm rather than routine admin SSH. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/400-aur-packages-hijacked-atomic-arch-campaign
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom deployment/orchestration scripts installed under /var/lib or a user's ~/.config wrapper that call scp/rsync
  • CI/CD runner or backup agent staged in /tmp or /var/lib performing rsync-over-ssh
  • Developer helper tools in ~/.config invoking git-over-ssh (partly excluded via git filter)
  • Config-management agents copying files to fleet hosts over ssh
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","rsnapshot","borg","restic","rclone") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gitlab-runner","buildkite-agent","jenkins")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent binary's path, hash, and the ssh/scp command line — note the destination host/user and whether a copy of the parent binary is being transferred. 2) Contain: isolate the source host, kill the process, and pre-emptively isolate the destination host(s) named in the command line; revoke/rotate the SSH keys used. 3) Hunt: on each destination host, hunt for the same persistence (systemd Restart=always, cron), the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process, and the campaign hashes; expand outward via known_hosts entries.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("ssh","scp","sftp","rsync")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/var/lib/","/tmp/","/.config/","/dev/shm/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git","ansible","ansible-playbook","bash","sh","zsh","fish","rsync","ssh","code")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/ssh","/scp","/sftp","/rsync")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/var/lib/","/tmp/","/.config/","/dev/shm/")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("/git","/ansible","/bash","/sh","/zsh","/fish","/rsync","/ssh"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| ParentImageFileName=/(\/var\/lib\/|\/tmp\/|\/\.config\/|\/dev\/shm\/)/i
| NOT ParentBaseFileName=/(git|ansible|bash|sh|zsh|fish|rsync|ssh)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentImageFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or SHA1 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or MD5 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or SHA1 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or MD5 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised Adform trackpoint-async.js clipper script by SHA256 on endpoint
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Online ad firm Adform’s script compromised to steal cryptocurrency
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 beacon to Adform clipper attacker server 84.32.102.230:7744 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
C2 beacon to Adform clipper attacker server 84.32.102.230:7744 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the attacker-controlled server (84.32.102.230, port 7744) that the trojanized Adform scripts beaconed to, exfiltrating victim IP, referring website and URL path. Any host reaching this IP indicates a browser that loaded the compromised trackpoint-async.js during the July 2026 supply-chain window. Rationale: 84.32.102.230:7744 is the attacker-controlled C2 confirmed in both Beaumont's DoublePulsar analysis and BleepingComputer; it is not owned by Adform and has no benign use, making any connection a high-fidelity indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002 T1115
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or malware sandbox intentionally detonating the IOC
  • Threat-intel scanner/crawler validating the C2 from an internal host
  • IP later reassigned to a benign shared-hosting tenant (verify port 7744 and date window July 2026)
  • Corporate VPN/proxy egress IP coincidentally matching (unlikely - it's a /32 attacker host)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host, user and initiating process for the connection; confirm it is a browser (chrome.exe/msedge.exe/firefox.exe) and whether the timestamp falls in the 26-27 July 2026 window. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at firewall/proxy, and if repeated beaconing is seen, isolate the host and force browser cache/cookie clearing per Adform's guidance. 3) Hunt: pivot to all other hosts that touched this IP, warn affected users to re-verify any crypto wallet addresses they copied/pasted recently, and check for the malicious script hash (see companion UC).

Compromised Adform trackpoint-async.js clipper script by SHA256 on endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunts the fleet for the exact malicious trojanized Adform tracking library (SHA256 02ff86c7...) landing on disk, typically as a browser cache artifact, to scope which endpoints downloaded the crypto-clipper during the supply-chain window. VirusTotal flagged this file clean across all engines, so hash-based hunting is required rather than AV signal. Rationale: SHA256 02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55 is the pre-extracted hash of the injected library; because VirusTotal shows zero detections, an exact-hash file hunt is the only reliable way to scope endpoint exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1115 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DFIR analyst intentionally saving the sample to an endpoint for analysis
  • A copy of the sample pulled from Beaumont's Pastebin/Archive.org for internal review
  • Malware-repo or IOC-feed clone stored on a workstation
  • SHA256 collision (cryptographically negligible - treat any exact match as true positive)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path (browser cache dir vs a saved copy) and the FileOriginUrl/downloading process to distinguish a real infection from analyst handling. 2) Contain: on genuine infections, clear the affected browser's cache/cookies as Adform advises, block 84.32.102.230, and advise the user to re-check any crypto addresses copied on 26-27 July 2026. 3) Hunt: correlate matching hosts against the C2-beacon UC, and search proxy logs for retrievals of trackpoint-async.js from s2.adform.net/a1.adform.net/ai1.adform.net during the window to build the full impacted-user list.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 == "02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 == "02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

DeviceProcessEvents

   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase

            - '-enc '

            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'

level: high

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or SHA1 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or MD5 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or SHA1 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or MD5 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-31 18 use cases 15 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Storm-2945, a sub-cluster of the Russian threat actor Midnight Blizzard, has been observed compromising the sign-in portals of hospitality-related organizations such as hotels since May 2026 in order to deliver malware to travelers and steal credentials in an operation we call CaptiveCrunch. The post CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix: browser-spawned interpreter downloading fake-update payload · [LLM] Captive-portal connectivity-check to browser-delivered executable download · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware deliver
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CornFlake RAT drop/execution from %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe · [LLM] CornFlake service persistence: 'svchost32' service / 'Cloud Sync Service' display name · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] CaptiveCrunch C2 / AiTM traffic to Storm-2945 doppelganger domains and IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Storm-2945 AiTM token replay: Entra sign-in from CaptiveCrunch actor IPs · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
CornFlake RAT drop/execution from %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts CaptiveCrunch's CornFlake Go RAT, which copies itself to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe in dropper mode. The nested svchost32\svchost32.exe path under a user profile is a near-unique CornFlake artifact and does not overlap with the legitimate system svchost.exe in System32. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim drop path %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe (code Block 3). The doubled directory+filename under a user profile is a high-fidelity CornFlake artifact distinct from legitimate System32\svchost.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer/test binary genuinely named svchost32.exe under a project folder (rare)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a monitored sandbox
  • Backup/EDR quarantine tooling re-creating the path during restore testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","mssense.exe","sense.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256 is unknown/unsigned and that FolderPath resolves under \AppData\Roaming\svchost32\; pull parent process (expect a browser or ClickFix-spawned interpreter). 2) Contain: isolate the device in Defender, kill the svchost32 process tree, and block the hash tenant-wide. 3) Hunt: pivot to the svchost32 service, Run keys and scheduled tasks on the host, and check outbound connections to the CaptiveCrunch C2 IP/domain list.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake service persistence: 'svchost32' service / 'Cloud Sync Service' display name AIInstallation High
Hunts CornFlake's Windows service persistence. It registers a service named svchost32 with display name 'Cloud Sync Service' and description 'Synchronizes files with the cloud storage provider' to masquerade as legitimate svchost.exe. These exact strings are article-unique. Rationale: Uses the article's exact persistence strings: service name svchost32, display name 'Cloud Sync Service', description 'Synchronizes files with the cloud storage provider' — a deliberate svchost.exe masquerade unlikely to appear in benign software. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate cloud-storage sync agent whose description mentions synchronizing files (validate the ServiceFileName path)
  • Internal software packaging that reuses a generic 'Cloud Sync Service' label
  • Backup restoration replaying old service-install events
Suppression filter
| where ServiceFileName has @"\AppData\" or ServiceFileName has @"\svchost32\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the service binary path resolves to the AppData svchost32 folder rather than a signed vendor path; verify the installing process. 2) Contain: stop and delete the svchost32 service, isolate host, block the binary hash. 3) Hunt: enumerate the host's Run keys, scheduled tasks and any watchdog process, and sweep the fleet for the same service name/display string.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\svchost32"
   or (RegistryValueName == "DisplayName" and RegistryValueData has "Cloud Sync Service")
   or (RegistryValueName == "Description" and RegistryValueData has "Synchronizes files with the cloud storage provider")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID in (4697, 7045)
| where ServiceName =~ "svchost32" or ServiceFileName has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, ServiceType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch C2 / AiTM traffic to Storm-2945 doppelganger domains and IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint connections to CaptiveCrunch actor infrastructure: the ms365/owa doppelganger domains and the six IOC IPs used for AiTM phishing and malware C2. Confirmed by Microsoft and ReliaQuest reporting on the same campaign. Rationale: Pre-extracted IOCs from the article (four ms365/owa doppelganger domains, six actor IPs) cross-checked against ReliaQuest's independent write-up of the same hospitality captive-portal campaign. Direct IOC matches are inherently high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox VMs deliberately resolving the IOCs during analysis
  • Security proxy or DNS sinkhole that logs the domain before blocking
  • IP reassignment — one of the six IPs later hosting benign infrastructure (revalidate freshness)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the connecting host and whether the user recently used hotel/conference Wi-Fi; capture full URL/SNI. 2) Contain: block all six IPs and four domains at proxy/firewall/DNS, isolate the host, and force-revoke the user's Entra sessions/tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot to that user's Entra sign-ins from the actor IPs (token replay) and search the host for the svchost32 CornFlake artifacts.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath

ClickFix: browser-spawned interpreter downloading fake-update payload AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the CaptiveCrunch ClickFix lure where a captive-portal-redirected browser session induces the user to run a copy-paste command, spawning powershell/cmd/mshta that fetches the fake 'browser/OS update' payload. Targets the browser→interpreter parent/child chain with download verbs in the command line. Rationale: The article names ClickFix as the primary delivery lure and describes fake browser/OS-update payloads fetched after user interaction. The browser→interpreter parent/child chain paired with download verbs is the article-specific execution signature (distinct from the generic 'Office spawns script' rule). Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1566.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer copy-pasting a PowerShell install one-liner (e.g. Chocolatey/winget bootstrap) from a webpage
  • IT self-service portals that launch cmd/powershell from a browser link
  • Browser-based remote-support tools that spawn scripted downloaders
  • Security-awareness simulation platforms replaying ClickFix lures
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("chocolatey.org","community.chocolatey.org","raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft","aka.ms") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full child command line — resolve the download URL and decode any Base64; check whether the URL is a Microsoft/vendor domain or a captive-portal-injected host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the interpreter tree, block the download URL/host. 3) Hunt: look for a follow-on write to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and connections to the CaptiveCrunch C2 list on the same device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","IWR","Invoke-RestMethod","DownloadString","DownloadFile","FromBase64String","certutil","curl","-EncodedCommand","-enc ","mshta")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","IWR","Invoke-RestMethod","DownloadString","DownloadFile","FromBase64String","certutil","curl","-EncodedCommand")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Captive-portal connectivity-check to browser-delivered executable download AIDelivery Medium
Hunts CaptiveCrunch's delivery mechanic where malware is served as a fake update 'in response to automated connectivity checks'. Flags a browser writing an executable/MSI/APK whose download referrer is one of the OS/browser NCSI connectivity-check endpoints — indicating a captive-portal MITM injected a payload into the check flow. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim NCSI connectivity-check endpoint list (code Block 1) as the download referrer. An executable delivered off the back of a connectivity check is the exact CaptiveCrunch fake-update mechanic and is not expressible as a simple single-event rule (referrer+file-type correlation), so Sigma/Datadog/Falcon are omitted where referrer telemetry isn't available. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1557 T1105 T1204.002
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate OS/driver update that happens to redirect through a connectivity endpoint (rare)
  • Enterprise captive-portal appliance legitimately serving a client agent
  • Browser test/telemetry tooling generating synthetic connectivity checks
  • Referrer stripped/rewritten by a corporate proxy, producing partial matches
Suppression filter
| where not (FileOriginUrl has_any ("microsoft.com","windowsupdate.com","mozilla.org","google.com") and SHA256 in~ ("") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the downloaded file's signature/hash and the referrer chain; correlate against whether the user was on hotel/airport Wi-Fi. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host if the binary is unsigned/unknown, block the serving host. 3) Hunt: check for execution of the file (→ svchost32 drop) and CaptiveCrunch C2 connections; alert other users who joined the same SSID/portal.
let ncsi_endpoints = dynamic(["msftconnecttest.com","edge-http.microsoft.com","msftncsi.com","captive.apple.com","connectivitycheck.gstatic.com","connectivitycheck.android.com","android.clients.google.com","www.gstatic.com","detectportal.firefox.com","detectportal.brave-http-only.com"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".msi" or FileName endswith ".apk" or FileName endswith ".dmg"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where FileOriginReferrerUrl has_any(ncsi_endpoints) or FileOriginUrl has_any(ncsi_endpoints)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Storm-2945 AiTM token replay: Entra sign-in from CaptiveCrunch actor IPs AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins originating from the six CaptiveCrunch actor IPs — the signature of AiTM/device-code token replay after credentials/tokens are harvested via the doppelganger portals. Covers the credential-access objective the campaign is built around. Rationale: Combines the article's six actor IPs with the device-code/AiTM tradecraft that Microsoft and Volexity document for the Storm-2372/Midnight Blizzard lineage. A successful Entra auth from known actor infrastructure is a direct token-replay indicator. Falcon left empty — Entra sign-ins are not in the FDR stream. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2025/02/13/multiple-russian-threat-actors-targeting-microsoft-device-code-authentication/
ATT&CKT1621 T1528 T1557
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IP reassignment where an actor IP later becomes a benign hosting/VPN egress (revalidate IOC freshness)
  • A security vendor proxy/CASB that egresses through one of these IPs during testing
  • Threat-intel researcher authenticating from the infrastructure in a lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, review the AppDisplayName/ResourceDisplayName (watch for 'Microsoft Authentication Broker' / device-registration), ClientApp and whether an interactive sign-in preceded it. 2) Contain: revoke the user's refresh tokens/sessions, force password reset + MFA re-registration, and remove any actor-registered Entra device. 3) Hunt: enumerate the user's mailbox rules and Graph/OAuth app grants for exfil, and check their endpoints for CornFlake artifacts.

| order by Timestamp desc

| where ResultType == 0
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, ClientAppUsed, AuthenticationRequirement, ConditionalAccessStatus, RiskLevelDuringSignIn
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] NocoBase anonymous auth:signUp followed by immediate myInAppChannels access (CVE-2026-52887 pre-exploit)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] NocoBase CVE-2026-52887 SQLi in myInAppChannels filter[latestMsgReceiveTimestamp][$lt]
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-52887: NocoBase: SQL injection in /api/myInAppChannel
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PostgreSQL 'postgres' process spawning a shell — CVE-2026-52887 COPY TO PROGRAM RCE
NocoBase CVE-2026-52887 SQLi in myInAppChannels filter[latestMsgReceiveTimestamp][$lt] AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP requests to NocoBase's /api/myInAppChannels:list where the filter's latestMsgReceiveTimestamp $lt operator carries SQL injection tokens (PG_SLEEP, stacked statements, COPY TO PROGRAM, CASE WHEN, UNION SELECT). This is the exact unescaped Sequelize.literal() sink described in the advisory, not a generic SQLi signature. Rationale: Anchors on the advisory's exact vulnerable field name (latestMsgReceiveTimestamp) plus endpoint (myInAppChannels) plus the confirmed injection primitives (PG_SLEEP, stacked ');', COPY TO PROGRAM) — the triple co-occurrence makes this near-zero FP outside pentests. Defender AH has no HTTP-request-content table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p849-8hwh-84j9
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test or sqlmap run against a NocoBase instance
  • Internal DAST/CI security scanner probing the API
  • Bug-bounty researcher testing the endpoint with benign PoC strings
  • A legitimate integration passing an ISO timestamp that happens to contain a matched keyword substring (rare — keywords are SQL-specific)
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "sqlmap" and SrcIpAddr !in (dynamic(["<internal_scanner_ip_placeholder_do_not_use>"]))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the source IP, the HTTP status, and whether the same IP first hit /api/auth:signUp and /api/auth:signIn minutes earlier (attacker obtains a member JWT before this request). Decode the filter query string and look for PG_SLEEP/stacked statements. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP at the WAF, revoke/rotate the offending member JWT and force-disable the self-registered account, and set allowSignUp:false on the auth-basic authenticator; upgrade the in-app-message plugin to >=2.0.61. 3) HUNT: On the Postgres/container host, hunt for postgres spawning a shell (UC3) and for any COPY ... TO PROGRAM output files (e.g. /tmp). Pull the users table and rotate the id=1 super-admin PBKDF2 hash if COPY exfil is suspected.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "myInAppChannels"
| where Url has "latestMsgReceiveTimestamp"
| where Url has_any ("pg_sleep","PG_SLEEP","TO PROGRAM","TO+PROGRAM","TO%20PROGRAM","CASE WHEN","CASE+WHEN","UNION SELECT","UNION+SELECT",");","%3B","--")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
