NocoBase anonymous auth:signUp followed by immediate myInAppChannels access (CVE-2026-52887 pre-exploit) AIDelivery Medium
Correlates a successful anonymous account creation at /api/auth:signUp (allowSignUp:true default) with an access to /api/myInAppChannels:list from the same source IP within 5 minutes. Captures the specific 'sign up then reach the loggedIn-ACL SQLi endpoint' precondition the advisory describes. Rationale: Uses the two advisory-named endpoints (auth:signUp with default allowSignUp:true, then myInAppChannels:list with loggedIn ACL) as a same-IP temporal pair — the fingerprint of an attacker bootstrapping a member account solely to reach the SQLi sink. Correlation is required (single-table can't express it), so no Sigma. Defender has no HTTP-content table. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p849-8hwh-84j9
ATT&CKT1078.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new user self-registers and immediately opens the in-app notifications panel (which calls myInAppChannels:list) — expected on sites that intentionally allow public signup
  • Shared corporate egress IP where one user signs up while another browses notifications
  • Load-test / synthetic monitoring that signs up then exercises the API
  • Mobile carrier CGNAT collapsing many users behind one source IP
Suppression filter
| where DelaySec <= 60 and Url has "latestMsgReceiveTimestamp"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full request sequence for the source IP; a benign new user hits myInAppChannels:list with no filter payload, an attacker follows with SQLi tokens (pivot to UC1). Check the created username and account age. 2) CONTAIN: If the myInAppChannels request carries injection syntax, block the IP, disable the new account, and set allowSignUp:false; patch to plugin >=2.0.61. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all accounts created via auth:signUp in the window, and review whether any reached data-returning collections or triggered COPY TO PROGRAM on the DB host.
let win = 5m;
let signups = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "auth:signUp"
    | where HttpStatusCode in ("200","201")
    | project SignupTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "myInAppChannels"
| join kind=inner signups on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (SignupTime .. SignupTime + win)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, SignupTime)
| project SignupTime, ChannelAccessTime = TimeGenerated, DelaySec, SrcIpAddr, Url, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by ChannelAccessTime desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as signupTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*auth:signUp*" AND Web.status IN ("200","201") by Web.src | join type=inner Web.src [ | tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as chanTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*myInAppChannels*" by Web.src ] | eval delaySec=chanTime-signupTime | where delaySec>=0 AND delaySec<=300 | eval firstTime=signupTime, lastTime=chanTime | convert ctime(signupTime) ctime(chanTime) | table src signupTime chanTime delaySec | sort - chanTime
| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as signupTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*auth:signUp*" AND Web.status IN ("200","201") by Web.src | join type=inner Web.src [ | tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as chanTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*myInAppChannels*" by Web.src ] | eval delaySec=chanTime-signupTime | where delaySec>=0 AND delaySec<=300 | eval firstTime=signupTime, lastTime=chanTime | convert ctime(signupTime) ctime(chanTime) | table src signupTime chanTime delaySec | sort - chanTime
PostgreSQL 'postgres' process spawning a shell — CVE-2026-52887 COPY TO PROGRAM RCE AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the database-server-side effect of the CVE-2026-52887 stacked-statement RCE: the superuser 'nocobase' role running COPY ... TO PROGRAM causes the postgres backend to fork /bin/sh. A postgres process spawning a shell is virtually never legitimate and confirms code execution as uid=999(postgres) inside the DB container. Rationale: Targets the advisory's confirmed RCE effect ('COPY ... TO PROGRAM runs shell as uid=999(postgres)') at the parent=postgres -> child=shell process edge, which is durable across payloads (unlike the PoC's /tmp/PWN_VERIFY.txt filenames). Corroborated by the well-documented Postgres COPY TO PROGRAM technique. Datadog linux.auditd's standard schema lacks a reliable parent-process field, so datadog_query is left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p849-8hwh-84j9 • https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/exploit/multi/postgres/postgres_copy_from_program_cmd_exec/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Postgres archive_command / restore_command configured to shell out to a script
  • Backup tooling (e.g. wal-g, pgBackRest) invoked as archive_command
  • A DBA legitimately using COPY ... TO PROGRAM for a scripted data pipeline
  • Container init/entrypoint wrappers that exec postgres and share the process name
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "archive_command" and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("wal-g","pgbackrest","pg_receivewal")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Capture the child shell's command line and its descendants on the DB host/container; correlate the timestamp with a preceding /api/myInAppChannels:list SQLi request (UC1) from the app tier. Confirm the DB role is superuser (POSTGRES_USER=nocobase on postgres:16 ships rolsuper). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the DB container, kill the attacker shell and children, rotate all DB credentials and the id=1 super-admin PBKDF2 hash, and drop the superuser attribute from the nocobase role (ALTER ROLE nocobase NOSUPERUSER). 3) HUNT: Look for files written by the shell (reverse shells, cron, SSH keys), outbound connections from the postgres process, and any COPY TO PROGRAM output artifacts in /tmp; review DB query logs for stacked statements if log_statement=all is enabled.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "postgres"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","busybox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "postgres"
| where ActingProcessName endswith "/sh" or ActingProcessName endswith "/bash" or ActingProcessName endswith "/dash" or ActingProcessName endswith "/ash" or ActingProcessName endswith "/busybox" or ActingProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","busybox")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Suspected Chinese-Speaking Hackers Target Central Asian Governments With OctLurk
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SilkLurk / PlugX DLL side-loading via signed NVIDIA/Realtek binaries · [LLM] GoogleUpDate scheduled task launching LurkProxy batch scripts · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy/PlugX C2 callback to campaign infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Impacket secretsdump / DCSync hash extraction via masquerading Adobe.exe · [LLM] AnyDesk-masquerading keylogger execution (OctLurk campaign) · [LLM] Fscan internal/public port scan with pp.txt credential file · [LLM] SilkLurk document staging and WinRAR/7-Zip archiving for exfiltration · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy/PlugX C2 callback to campaign infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts host connections to the hard-coded C2 domains and IPs Kaspersky attributes to the OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy/PlugX campaign against Central Asian governments. OctLurk beacons to dns.multitoconference.com, LurkProxy to 154.196.162.76 (SOCKS5 listener on 64980), SilkLurk/PlugX to *.kozow.com and 64.7.198.130. Any internal host touching these is high-confidence compromise. Rationale: Uses the exact C2 domains/IPs from the article's IOC block, confirmed and mapped per-family (OctLurk=dns.multitoconference.com/45.138.157.165, LurkProxy=dns.ssentialserv.xyz/154.196.162.76:64980, SilkLurk/PlugX=*.kozow.com/64.7.198.130) via the Securelist report — every hit is a named-IOC match, not a heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/suspected-chinese-speaking-hackers.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.001 T1008
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • digital.leroymerlin.com is a legitimate-looking retail-brand string reused as attacker infra — a real Leroy Merlin corporate host resolving it would be benign; scope to org-internal government/enterprise assets
  • Security researcher / sandbox VM in the environment intentionally detonating the sample
  • Threat-intel platform or proxy pre-fetching/validating the IOC domains
  • DNS sinkhole or RPZ appliance logging the block as a resolution event
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("threatintel-fetcher.exe") or DeviceName has "malware-lab")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — a signed NVIDIA/Realtek binary (side-load loader) or a .bat is high-confidence; capture the resolving process tree and the exact IOC hit. 2) Contain: isolate the host in Defender/Falcon, block the domain/IP at proxy and firewall, and force-revoke any interactive sessions on that host. 3) Hunt: pivot on DeviceId for the other campaign UCs (secretsdump/Adobe.exe, AnyDesk keylogger, fscan, vulkan-1.dll side-load, GoogleUpDate task) and enumerate all hosts that resolved any domain in the list over the last 90 days.

Impacket secretsdump / DCSync hash extraction via masquerading Adobe.exe AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the campaign's domain-controller credential dump: Kaspersky observed an Impacket secretsdump.py port dropped as Adobe.exe (MD5 32a5985543433a4f60da2fafd873b927) run through OctLurk's command-shell plugin to harvest hashes from DCs. Anchors on the known hash plus Impacket -just-dc / target@host command syntax. Rationale: Combines the Securelist-confirmed MD5 (32a5985543433a4f60da2fafd873b927, the Adobe.exe secretsdump port) with Impacket's distinctive -just-dc / user@target invocation, so it catches both the exact dropped binary and any recompiled variant. Not covered by the excluded LSASS/PsExec rules — this is DCSync/NTDS extraction. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/
ATT&CKT1003.006 T1003.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team / pentest engagement legitimately running Impacket secretsdump against a DC
  • Backup or AD migration tooling referencing NTDS.dit in its command line
  • DC recovery / ntdsutil IFM export by a domain admin (would show ntdsutil, not -just-dc)
  • Security product self-test invoking a benign secretsdump string
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pentest","redteam") or AccountName in~ ("svc-adbackup"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target host is or connects to a Domain Controller and whether the account is an admin; a non-admin or service account running -just-dc is immediately critical. Pull the MD5 and parent process. 2) Contain: isolate the source host, disable the executing account, and force a krbtgt double-reset plan review if DC hashes were dumped. 3) Hunt: treat all domain hashes as compromised; hunt for the campaign's fscan/pp.txt lateral movement, AnyDesk keylogger, and C2 domains on the same host and any DC touched.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where MD5 == "32a5985543433a4f60da2fafd873b927"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("secretsdump","-just-dc","-just-dc-ntlm","NTDS.dit")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "-just-dc" and ProcessCommandLine has "@")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has_any ("secretsdump","-just-dc","-just-dc-ntlm","NTDS.dit")
   or (CommandLine has "-just-dc" and CommandLine has "@")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AnyDesk-masquerading keylogger execution (OctLurk campaign) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the campaign's keylogger that Kaspersky reports masquerades as AnyDesk to evade detection (dropped as AnyDesk.exe, MD5 2a571f6cee42a17d873f4c942649813f). Fires on the known hash, or on any AnyDesk.exe whose signer isn't 'AnyDesk Software GmbH' or that runs outside the legitimate install path. Rationale: Anchors on the Securelist-confirmed keylogger hash (2a571f6cee42a17d873f4c942649813f) plus the article's explicit 'keylogger masquerades as AnyDesk' behaviour, using signer/path mismatch so a recompiled variant still trips. Distinct from generic keylogging rules by requiring the AnyDesk name/hash pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/
ATT&CKT1056.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/standalone AnyDesk run from Downloads or a USB by a legitimate remote-support tech (path mismatch, but valid signer — filtered by the company-name check on Defender)
  • AnyDesk MSI installer staging the binary in a temp folder mid-install
  • IT helpdesk custom-repackaged AnyDesk with an altered path
  • Renamed legitimate AnyDesk used to bypass a corporate app blocklist
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName == "AnyDesk Software GmbH" and MD5 != "2a571f6cee42a17d873f4c942649813f")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName and code-signing status — a blank/invalid signer or the exact MD5 is a true positive; validate whether real AnyDesk is sanctioned on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, capture the binary for the keylog output file, and reset credentials for the logged-on user (keylogging = likely password capture). 3) Hunt: correlate on DeviceId for secretsdump (Adobe.exe), browser-credential theft, and C2 callbacks; review the user's authentications since first execution for reuse of captured creds.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where MD5 == "2a571f6cee42a17d873f4c942649813f"
   or (FileName =~ "anydesk.exe"
       and (ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "AnyDesk Software GmbH"
            or FolderPath !has "\\Program Files"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\anydesk.exe"
| where NewProcessName !has "\\Program Files\\AnyDesk\\" and NewProcessName !has "\\Program Files (x86)\\AnyDesk\\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fscan internal/public port scan with pp.txt credential file AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the campaign's network reconnaissance: OctLurk's shell plugin runs Fscan to scan internal and public ranges for SSH (22) and MySQL (3306), then attempts access with credentials from a file named pp.txt. Anchors on the fscan binary, its -pwdf password-file flag, and the pp.txt filename. Rationale: Uses the article's named tool (Fscan) and the highly specific pp.txt credential filename plus fscan's -pwdf flag — the pp.txt string alone is essentially unique to this campaign, and fscan is a known Chinese-APT scanner, giving very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1046 T1595.001 T1110.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized internal vulnerability scan or asset-discovery sweep using fscan by the security team
  • Pentest engagement bringing fscan as a tool
  • A benign file coincidentally named pp.txt referenced by unrelated software (rare; pair with fscan/-pwdf)
  • Network engineer troubleshooting connectivity to port 22/3306 with a scripted checker
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("vulnscan","asset-inventory") or DeviceName startswith "SEC-SCANNER")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process is fscan (hash/path) and whether the scan is authorized; extract the target ranges and the pp.txt contents to scope which hosts/creds were targeted. 2) Contain: isolate the scanning host, rotate any credentials present in pp.txt, and alert on SSH/MySQL auth from the host to internal 22/3306. 3) Hunt: review DeviceLogonEvents and MySQL/SSH auth logs for successful logons from the source host to scanned targets, and pivot to the campaign's secretsdump and C2 UCs on the same DeviceId.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName has "fscan"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("fscan","pp.txt","-pwdf")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where NewProcessName has "fscan" or CommandLine has_any ("fscan","pp.txt","-pwdf")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SilkLurk / PlugX DLL side-loading via signed NVIDIA/Realtek binaries AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the campaign's DLL side-load chain: signed NVIDIA (NetSetSvc.exe, nvgwls.exe) and Realtek (RtkSmbus.exe, RtkNGUI64.exe) executables loading attacker DLLs (nvml.dll, vulkan-1.dll, RtkSmbusLoc.dll, RtkNGUI64Loc.dll) to run SilkLurk/PlugX in memory, plus OctLurk's oleasapi.dll/msbasesysdc.dll loaders. Targets the specific loader-DLL names and paths from Kaspersky. Rationale: Built entirely from Securelist's DLL side-load table (NetSetSvc.exe+nvml.dll, nvgwls.exe/RtkSmbus/RtkNGUI64 pairs) and the exact OctLurk loader DLL names/paths (oleasapi.dll, msbasesysdc.dll, vulkan-1.dll in OneDrive setup / System32\0409 / nvcontainer plugins). vulkan-1.dll is a legit filename so it is path-gated to avoid FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1055.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine NVIDIA/Realtek driver components loading their real DLLs from Program Files (excluded by the co-named/path gating)
  • A legitimate vulkan-1.dll shipped by a game/GPU app outside the three flagged paths (path filter suppresses this)
  • Software-distribution tooling staging DLLs into ProgramData during an install
  • Security-tool DLLs coincidentally named oleasapi.dll (these names are not real Windows components, so effectively never legitimate)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Program Files\\" and FileName =~ "vulkan-1.dll" and FolderPath has "\\Program Files\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host binary is the signed NVIDIA/Realtek exe but running from a user-writable/staging path (side-load tell), and grab the loaded DLL's hash and folder. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the DLL and its co-located EXE, and snapshot memory (SilkLurk/PlugX run in memory). 3) Hunt: pivot on DeviceId for the C2 domains (SilkLurk=*.kozow.com, PlugX=gycudore.kozow.com/64.7.198.130), the GoogleUpDate task, and cross-check the shared staging directory for OctLurk co-infection.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("NetSetSvc.exe","nvgwls.exe","RtkSmbus.exe","RtkNGUI64.exe")
         and FileName in~ ("nvml.dll","vulkan-1.dll","RtkSmbusLoc.dll","RtkNGUI64Loc.dll"))
   or FileName in~ ("oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll")
   or (FileName =~ "vulkan-1.dll" and FolderPath has_any (@"\ProgramData\Microsoft OneDrive\setup\", @"\System32\0409\", @"\nvidia corporation\display.nvcontainer\plugins\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("nvml.dll","RtkSmbusLoc.dll","RtkNGUI64Loc.dll","oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll")
   or (TargetFileName =~ "vulkan-1.dll" and TargetFilePath has_any ("Microsoft OneDrive\\setup","System32\\0409","display.nvcontainer\\plugins"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileMD5
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SilkLurk document staging and WinRAR/7-Zip archiving for exfiltration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts SilkLurk's collection step: cmd.exe launches PowerShell to mount admin shares, stage confidential documents, then archive them with WinRAR/7-Zip before exfil. Anchors on archive utilities spawned from cmd/PowerShell using add-archive and password flags, the tell of staged-data compression. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit SilkLurk sequence (cmd -> PowerShell -> mount admin share -> stage docs -> WinRAR/7-Zip archive) via the archive-utility + password-flag + script-parent combination, which is the compression tell of staged data prior to exfil rather than a generic WinRAR launch. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/suspected-chinese-speaking-hackers.html
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1039 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/backup script legitimately zipping logs or share content with 7-Zip from a scheduled cmd job
  • Developer build pipeline invoking 7z a from a PowerShell wrapper
  • IT packaging software into password-protected archives for distribution
  • User compressing a folder via WinRAR right-click (parent would be explorer.exe, largely excluded by the script-parent filter)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("backup","\\Jenkins\\","build.ps1") or ProcessCommandLine has "\\Logs\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the archive command for source paths pointing at admin shares (\\host\C$, sensitive doc folders) and a password flag; confirm the parent cmd/PowerShell lineage and the acting user. 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the archive output file, and block outbound to the campaign C2/proxy IPs to stop exfil. 3) Hunt: look for preceding net use to admin shares and following uploads to 154.196.162.76 (LurkProxy) or the *.kozow.com C2; check other hosts the same account staged data from.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("rar.exe","winrar.exe","7z.exe","7za.exe","7zg.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" a "," a -","-hp"," -p")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\rar.exe","\\winrar.exe","\\7z.exe","\\7za.exe","\\7zg.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any (" a "," a -","-hp"," -p")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoogleUpDate scheduled task launching LurkProxy batch scripts AIInstallation High
Hunts the campaign's persistence/launch mechanism: attackers register a scheduled task named GoogleUpDate that runs batch scripts (\Windows\Temp\in.bat, \Videos\1.bat, \Desktop\auto.bat) responsible for launching LurkProxy after checking connectivity to dns.ssentialserv.xyz. Anchors on the distinctive task name and batch-script paths. Rationale: Anchors on the Securelist-confirmed scheduled-task name 'GoogleUpDate' (note the non-standard capitalisation, unlike the real GoogleUpdate service) and the three exact batch-script paths that launch LurkProxy, making this a near-unique campaign fingerprint with minimal legitimate overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Google Update scheduled tasks (named 'GoogleUpdateTaskMachine...' — different casing/pattern, largely excluded)
  • Admin ad-hoc batch scripts coincidentally named 1.bat/auto.bat outside the flagged paths
  • Software installer creating a temp .bat in \Windows\Temp during setup
  • IT deployment tooling registering a maintenance task
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpdateTaskMachine" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "GoogleUpdate.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the task name is exactly 'GoogleUpDate' (attacker casing) and read the referenced .bat contents; check whether it references LurkProxy or the connectivity check to dns.ssentialserv.xyz. 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task, isolate the host, quarantine the batch scripts and any LurkProxy binary, and block 154.196.162.76 / dns.ssentialserv.xyz. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for a GoogleUpDate task and the three batch paths, and pivot on DeviceId to the OctLurk C2 and DLL side-load UCs for full-chain confirmation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Windows\Temp\in.bat", @"\Videos\1.bat", @"\Desktop\auto.bat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
   or CommandLine has_any (@"\Windows\Temp\in.bat", @"\Videos\1.bat", @"\Desktop\auto.bat")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents

2026-07-31 2 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An AI agent published a malicious package to PyPI and 15 systems ran it within an hour. What Anthropic's incident means for supply chain security.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children

status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows

    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'

            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Malicious vault-addr annotation on ConfigMap/Secret pointing at cloud metadata (CVE-2026-54725) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts ConfigMap/Secret create/update admission events carrying the vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-addr annotation whose value targets a cloud metadata endpoint (IMDS 169.254.169.254, ECS 169.254.170.2, GCP metadata.google.internal, Alibaba 100.100.200.200), localhost, or that pairs with vault-skip-verify=true. This is the exact SSRF trigger for CVE-2026-54725 in bank-vaults vault-secrets-webhook <=1.22.2 (fixed 1.23.1). Rationale: Pivots on the exact CVE annotation key vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-addr plus the concrete PoC IMDS target 169.254.169.254 and the vault-skip-verify=true evasion flag named in the advisory; a legit override never points a per-object annotation at link-local metadata. Cross-checked GitLab GLAD, the GHSA, and bank-vaults mutating-webhook docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r2v3-8gwf-7ghm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/bank-vaults/vault-secrets-webhook/CVE-2026-54725/ • https://bank-vaults.dev/docs/mutating-webhook/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.005
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Platform team legitimately overriding vault-addr per-namespace to an in-cluster Vault (10.x/ClusterIP) — excluded because query only fires on metadata/localhost targets
  • A GitOps tool re-applying an existing benign ConfigMap that already carried a vault-addr override to the real Vault
  • Security scanner or admission-policy test harness deliberately submitting the PoC manifest (validate against change ticket)
  • Developer copy-pasting a sample manifest that still contains a localhost vault-addr placeholder
  • vault-skip-verify=true set legitimately in a dev/test namespace with self-signed internal Vault
Suppression filter
| where not (VaultAddr matches regex @"(?i)^https?://(10\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|192\.168\.)" and SkipVerify != "true")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full audit record for the AuditId and read the vault-addr value and requesting user.username; if it resolves to IMDS/localhost/attacker infra it is malicious, not a misconfig. 2) Contain: delete the offending ConfigMap/Secret, revoke create/update on ConfigMaps+Secrets for the user in that namespace, and if webhook <1.23.1 gate admission or scale the webhook to 0 until patched to 1.23.1. 3) Hunt: enumerate every ConfigMap/Secret carrying a vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-addr annotation cluster-wide, and pivot to UC2/UC3 to see if a TokenRequest fired or the webhook egressed to the address.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where Stage == "ResponseComplete"
| extend Resource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource)
| where Resource in ("configmaps","secrets")
| extend Ann = parse_json(RequestObject).metadata.annotations
| extend VaultAddr = tostring(Ann["vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-addr"])
| where isnotempty(VaultAddr)
| extend SkipVerify = tostring(Ann["vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-skip-verify"])
| extend VaultSA = tostring(Ann["vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-serviceaccount"])
| where VaultAddr has_any ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2","metadata.google.internal","100.100.200.200","127.0.0.1","localhost")
     or SkipVerify =~ "true"
| project TimeGenerated, Username, UserAgent, Resource, Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), Name = tostring(ObjectRef.name), VaultAddr, SkipVerify, VaultSA
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious vault-addr Annotation Pointing at Cloud Metadata on ConfigMap or Secret
id: 4b2f9c11-7d3a-4e58-9a1f-2c6e5d8b0a41
description: Detects CVE-2026-54725 SSRF trigger where a ConfigMap or Secret is admitted with the bank-vaults vault-addr annotation pointing at a cloud metadata endpoint, localhost, or paired with vault-skip-verify=true.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r2v3-8gwf-7ghm
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/bank-vaults/vault-secrets-webhook/CVE-2026-54725/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/01
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1552.005
logsource:
  product: kubernetes
  service: audit
detection:
  selection:
    verb:
      - create
      - update
      - patch
    objectRef.resource:
      - configmaps
      - secrets
  annotation:
    - 'vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-addr'
  targets:
    - '169.254.169.254'
    - '169.254.170.2'
    - 'metadata.google.internal'
    - '100.100.200.200'
  condition: selection and annotation and targets
level: high
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.resource:(configmaps OR secrets) "banzaicloud.io/vault-addr" ("169.254.169.254" OR "169.254.170.2" OR "metadata.google.internal" OR "100.100.200.200" OR "vault-skip-verify")
# log group: /aws/eks/*/cluster  (EKS kube-apiserver-audit control-plane log stream)
fields @timestamp, verb, objectRef.resource, objectRef.namespace, objectRef.name, user.username, @message
| filter verb in ["create","update","patch"]
      and objectRef.resource in ["configmaps","secrets"]
      and @message like /vault\.security\.banzaicloud\.io\/vault-addr/
      and (@message like /169\.254\.169\.254/ or @message like /169\.254\.170\.2/ or @message like /metadata\.google\.internal/ or @message like /100\.100\.200\.200/ or @message like /vault-skip-verify/)
| sort @timestamp desc
CLOUD
index=* (sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" OR sourcetype="kubernetes_audit") verb IN ("create","update","patch") "objectRef.resource" IN ("configmaps","secrets") "vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-addr"
| spath
| rename "requestObject.metadata.annotations.vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-addr" AS vault_addr, "requestObject.metadata.annotations.vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-skip-verify" AS skip_verify, "requestObject.metadata.annotations.vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-serviceaccount" AS vault_sa
| where isnotnull(vault_addr) AND (like(vault_addr,"%169.254.169.254%") OR like(vault_addr,"%169.254.170.2%") OR like(vault_addr,"%metadata.google.internal%") OR like(vault_addr,"%100.100.200.200%") OR like(vault_addr,"%127.0.0.1%") OR like(vault_addr,"%localhost%") OR skip_verify="true")
| table _time user.username objectRef.namespace objectRef.name vault_addr skip_verify vault_sa
| sort - _time
vault-secrets-webhook ServiceAccount TokenRequest fan-out (cluster-wide SA token theft, CVE-2026-54725) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the vault-secrets-webhook ServiceAccount minting JWTs via the serviceaccounts/token subresource (TokenRequest API) for multiple distinct ServiceAccounts in a short window — the crown-jewel impact of CVE-2026-54725 where the webhook's cluster-wide serviceaccounts/token:create is abused to fetch high-priv SA tokens for exfiltration. Rationale: Keys on the exact abuse primitive the advisory names — the webhook's cluster-wide serviceaccounts/token:create surfaced as create on the /serviceaccounts/<name>/token subresource by the vault-secrets-webhook identity — and adds a distinct-SA fan-out threshold to separate benign per-pod injection from mass token harvesting. Corroborated via GHSA and GitLab GLAD. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r2v3-8gwf-7ghm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/bank-vaults/vault-secrets-webhook/CVE-2026-54725/
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Busy cluster where the webhook legitimately injects Vault secrets into many pods at once (deployment rollout) causing genuine token fan-out — tune threshold up per baseline
  • kubelet node-level token rotation (system:node:*) — excluded by the vault-secrets-webhook username filter
  • Other CSI/secrets-store drivers using bound tokens in the same namespace
  • Autoscaling event spinning up many replicas that each trigger legitimate SA token creation
  • Cluster with a single high-churn namespace where 3 distinct SAs in 10m is normal — raise DistinctSAs threshold
Suppression filter
| where Username !startswith "system:node:" and Username !has "csi-secrets-store"
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the target ServiceAccounts (SampleSAs) and check whether any are high-privilege (cluster-admin bindings, Vault-role-bound); correlate the same 10m window with UC1 (suspicious vault-addr annotation) and UC3 (egress). 2) Contain: rotate/invalidate the minted SA tokens (delete+recreate the SAs or bump their token audiences), revoke the webhook's cluster-wide serviceaccounts/token:create by scoping the ClusterRole, and patch to 1.23.1. 3) Hunt: for each target SA, review Vault audit logs for logins from the webhook pod's egress IP and any secret reads under that role; assume compromise of any secret the SA role could read.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Verb == "create"
| where RequestUri matches regex @"/api/v1/namespaces/[^/]+/serviceaccounts/[^/]+/token"
| where Username has "vault-secrets-webhook"
| extend TargetSA = extract(@"/serviceaccounts/([^/]+)/token", 1, RequestUri)
| extend NS = extract(@"/namespaces/([^/]+)/serviceaccounts", 1, RequestUri)
| summarize TokenCount = count(), DistinctSAs = dcount(strcat(NS,"/",TargetSA)), SampleSAs = make_set(strcat(NS,"/",TargetSA), 25) by Username, UserAgent, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctSAs >= 3   // webhook minting tokens for 3+ distinct SAs in 10m is abnormal fan-out
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:create @objectRef.resource:serviceaccounts @objectRef.subresource:token @user.username:*vault-secrets-webhook*
# log group: /aws/eks/*/cluster  (EKS kube-apiserver-audit control-plane log stream)
fields @timestamp, user.username, objectRef.namespace, objectRef.name, sourceIPs.0
| filter verb = "create" and objectRef.resource = "serviceaccounts" and objectRef.subresource = "token" and user.username like /vault-secrets-webhook/
| stats count(*) as tokenReqs, count_distinct(objectRef.name) as distinctSAs by user.username, bin(10m)
| filter distinctSAs >= 3
| sort distinctSAs desc
CLOUD
index=* (sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" OR sourcetype="kubernetes_audit") verb=create "objectRef.resource"=serviceaccounts "objectRef.subresource"=token "user.username"="*vault-secrets-webhook*"
| bucket _time span=10m
| stats dc('objectRef.name') AS distinctSAs values('objectRef.name') AS targetSAs values('objectRef.namespace') AS namespaces count by _time "user.username"
| where distinctSAs>=3
| sort - _time
vault-secrets-webhook pod egress to cloud metadata / IMDS (SSRF exfil, CVE-2026-54725) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the vault-secrets-webhook process making an outbound connection to a cloud metadata endpoint (IMDS 169.254.169.254, ECS 169.254.170.2, Alibaba 100.100.200.200) — the SSRF egress that CVE-2026-54725 forces during admission when an attacker-supplied vault-addr points at metadata. An admission controller has no legitimate reason to reach link-local IMDS. Rationale: Uses the concrete PoC destination 169.254.169.254 (plus ECS/Alibaba metadata equivalents) tied to the vault-secrets-webhook process image — an admission controller reaching link-local IMDS is the observable SSRF payload of CVE-2026-54725. Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: no per-pod netflow source is documented for Datadog here and AWS deliberately omits 169.254.169.254 traffic from VPC Flow Logs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r2v3-8gwf-7ghm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/bank-vaults/vault-secrets-webhook/CVE-2026-54725/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node/pod legitimately using IMDS for IAM credentials when IRSA/pod-identity is not configured — but the webhook binary specifically should never do this
  • Sidecar or init container sharing the webhook pod network namespace calling IMDS (validate initiating process)
  • Cloud SDK health probe from the same host mis-attributed to the webhook by a coarse flow logger
  • Monitoring/metadata-scraping DaemonSet on the node (excluded by the process-image filter)
  • Migration to IMDSv2 producing PUT token-fetch traffic to IMDS during normal SDK init
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the InitiatingProcess is the vault-secrets-webhook binary and note the exact RemoteUrl/path (a /v1/auth/<path>/login POST or /latest/meta-data path confirms the SSRF chain); check the same window for UC1's malicious annotation. 2) Contain: isolate/cordon the node or scale the webhook to 0, and on EKS enforce IMDSv2 (hop limit 1) plus block pod access to 169.254.169.254 via network policy; patch to 1.23.1. 3) Hunt: review the cloud IAM role attached to the webhook pod/node for any API calls made with harvested IMDS credentials, and inspect Vault audit logs for logins originating from the webhook egress IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2","100.100.200.200")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "vault-secrets-webhook" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "vault-secrets-webhook"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2","100.100.200.200") or DstHostname =~ "metadata.google.internal"
| where SrcHostname has "vault-secrets-webhook" or SrcUsername has "vault-secrets-webhook"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hunts the memory-disclosure exploitation Unit 42 confirmed against Citrix NetScaler: a source IP hammering the SAML IdP /saml/login endpoint in a tight loop to repeatedly overread heap memory and harvest session cookies. Normal SAML SSO produces a handful of /saml/login hits per user; 50+ from one IP in 10 minutes is a memory-scrape loop. Rationale: Grounds on the corroborated CVE-2026-3055 exploit path: unauthenticated crafted SAMLRequest to /saml/login (AssertionConsumerServiceURL omitted) leaking heap via NSC_TASS. The loop-volume threshold captures the repeated-overread behaviour needed to reassemble cookies. defender_kql/datadog/falcon empty: a NetScaler appliance is not onboarded to Defender XDR/FDR and inbound appliance web logs have no clean Datadog source; the detection lives in CEF (Sentinel) and the CIM Web datamodel (Splunk). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-3055/ • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-3055-netscaler-memory-disclosure/ • https://github.com/rapid7/metasploit-framework/pull/21204 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chinese-hacker-commands-deepseek-via.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1212
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scan (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) hitting the SAML endpoint in bulk
  • Corporate egress NAT concentrating many real SSO users behind one public IP during a morning login storm
  • SSO gateway / load-balancer health probes polling /saml/login
  • SAML federation partner proxy relaying many users' auth from a single IP
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","masscan","zgrab","Expanse")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP's full /saml/login request stream — confirm the requests carry SAMLRequest bodies missing AssertionConsumerServiceURL and check NetScaler version against the CVE-2026-3055 patched build; look for abnormally large responses. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the ADC/WAF, and if the appliance is unpatched and SAML-IdP-configured, take it out of rotation and rotate all AAA/LDAP bind credentials and session secrets that could have been in memory. 3) Hunt: enumerate every NSC_AAAC/NSC_TASS session active after the scrape window and pivot to UC2 (cookie reuse) to find hijacked sessions; review authentication logs for the leaked accounts.

| where DeviceVendor has "Citrix" or DeviceProduct has_any ("NetScaler","ADC","Gateway")

| where RequestCount > 50   // 50+ /saml/login hits in 10m from one IP = CVE-2026-3055 memory-scrape loop, not normal SAML SSO

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Network communication with Iranian-APT infrastructure targeting Rockwell PLCs (185.82.73.160-171 / 135.136.1.133) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any inbound or outbound network flow to the ULTAHOST operator workstation range (185.82.73.160-171, AS214036) or the M247 staging box (135.136.1.133, AS9009) tied by CISA/Censys to the coordinated attacks on U.S. water-sector PLCs. High-fidelity because these are dedicated single-purpose attacker hosts, not shared services. Rationale: Uses the exact attacker IPs from the article's IOC block, refined against the Censys bundle (12 IPs across the ULTAHOST /28 operator range plus the M247 single-use staging box). Dedicated attacker infrastructure = near-zero-FP alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://censys.com/blog/iranian-affiliated-apt-targeting-rockwell-allen-bradley-plcs/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/30/cisa-urges-water-and-wastewater-systems-sector-protect-ot-against-activity-targeting-plcs • https://www.fbi.gov/news/press-releases/malicious-cyber-actors-targeting-water-and-wastewater-sector-internet--facing-programmable-logic-controllers-causing-operational-disruptions
ATT&CKT0883 T0886 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internet-wide scanners or threat-intel crawlers (Shodan/Censys/Shadowserver) that happen to be re-homed onto the same ULTAHOST /28 after attacker teardown
  • A security researcher or your own red team pivoting through a rented ULTAHOST/M247 VPS in the same range
  • Threat-intel platform (e.g. MISP/VT) sandbox detonations reaching out to the IPs from an analyst subnet
  • Legitimate SaaS re-provisioned onto a recycled ULTAHOST IP months later (infra churn)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal asset (DeviceName/SourceIP) and whether the flow is inbound (attempted access to an exposed PLC/HMI/engineering box) or outbound (possible beacon); pull the port — 44818/2222/43589 or RDP raise severity. 2) Contain: block the IP set at the perimeter and OT DMZ firewall in both directions, isolate the internal host, and pull the affected PLC's known-good image offline per Rockwell's MicroLogix 1400 recovery notice in case credentials were changed. 3) Hunt: sweep 30d of firewall/EDR for any of the 12 IPs, for inbound EtherNet/IP on TCP 44818 to OT subnets, and for unexpected RDP to non-standard ports; validate no PLC IP/password changes occurred.

Inbound EtherNet/IP (TCP 44818) or TCP 2222 to OT assets from the public internet AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces the exact exposure CISA warns about: internet-reachable Rockwell/Allen-Bradley PLCs (and HMIs) accepting EtherNet/IP (TCP 44818) or TCP 2222 connections directly from public source addresses — the vector the Iranian-affiliated actors used to reach MicroLogix 1400 / CompactLogix / Micro850 controllers and change their IPs and passwords. Durable even after attacker IPs rotate. Rationale: Pivots on EtherNet/IP TCP 44818 (plus the TCP 2222 secondary target) confirmed by the Censys write-up as the protocol/ports the actors used against exposed Rockwell controllers; scoping to public source IPs isolates the internet-exposure condition CISA/FBI told operators to eliminate. Firewall CEF is the primary source since PLCs don't run EDR; Defender clause covers Rockwell engineering/HMI Windows hosts that also listen on 44818. Cross-checked against: • https://censys.com/blog/iranian-affiliated-apt-targeting-rockwell-allen-bradley-plcs/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/30/cisa-urges-water-and-wastewater-systems-sector-protect-ot-against-activity-targeting-plcs • https://www.securityweek.com/cisa-urges-water-sector-to-protect-ot-after-coordinated-attacks-on-plcs/
ATT&CKT0883 T0819 T0886
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized remote SCADA integrator/vendor connecting over a public IP because a site-to-site VPN was down or misconfigured
  • Internet background-noise scanners (Shodan, Censys, Shadowserver, academic scanners) probing TCP 44818
  • Carrier-grade NAT / cellular-modem egress making a legitimately-internal engineering host appear to have a public peer
  • Scheduled penetration test or attack-surface-management scan against the OT DMZ
  • A cloud-hosted historian/telemetry gateway legitimately polling PLCs over EtherNet/IP across a public link
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("198.20.69.0/24","198.20.70.0/24","66.240.192.0/18","71.6.128.0/17","185.163.109.0/24") // exclude Shodan/Censys/Shadowserver research scanner ranges
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the DestinationIP is an OT asset (PLC/HMI/engineering station) and whether the SourceIP is a known integrator/scanner; any public source touching 44818 on a controller is treated as exposure until proven otherwise. 2) Contain: remove the asset from direct internet exposure (front it with VPN/gateway per CISA), apply an IP allow-list on the firewall, and change default/known passwords; verify the PLC image against a known-good backup. 3) Hunt: enumerate every OT asset with inbound 44818/2222/VNC(5900)/Telnet(23) from public space, cross-check those SourceIPs against the 185.82.73.160-171 and 135.136.1.133 IOCs, and review PLC config-change/loss-of-comms events around first-seen.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort in (44818, 2222)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

HollowFrame Loader Deploys Matryoshka Backdoor in Spear-Phishing Attack on Law Firm

The Hacker News
2026-07-31 17 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have shed light on a previously undocumented Go-based loader framework called HollowFrame and a Rust-based malware family tracked as Matryoshka. According to Blackpoint Cyber, the intrusion sequence begins with a spear-phishing message containing a link to an encrypted archive, which holds a Windows Shortcut (LNK). Executing the file triggers a multi-stage chain that

Exploitation. HollowFrame LNK delivery: cmd.exe writes payload, certutil -decode to .cmd, PowerShell fetch AIDelivery High
Hunts the HollowFrame 'Case Documents' LNK execution chain in which explorer-spawned cmd.exe writes a payload, certutil.exe decodes it to a .cmd, and a second cmd.exe /K launches PowerShell to pull next-stage code. Anchored on the certutil -decode-to-.cmd step, which is rare in benign use and is the pivot shown in Blackpoint's process-tree diagram. Rationale: Uses the exact certutil -decode-to-.cmd step and explorer/cmd parentage from the article's process-tree image (cmd.png); certutil writing a .cmd under an interactive shell is high-fidelity and near-never benign. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/paperwork-to-payload-from-shortcut-clicks-to-rundll32-execution/ • https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhEQz5wx5Wk3F3uCiiNzfwmlWu3vgQN2TohgoaIdhGjyVcu05SfUmZjzmClUPOkK9M6-S06GZJ4jDqesb_2AYetLTuebp9_K8-Dkfp88cjAJYrzNhyPBwTJ_CD1gWAGuo0cnEz7Mx8eb1r0A5_gv6xsACyEPByhr-COEjfyVn1lIBEJNHK44Vfk7EHCtmHK/s1700-e365/cmd.png
ATT&CKT1140 T1059.001 T1204.002 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit software installers using certutil to decode embedded config into a .cmd (rare)
  • Admin scripts that base64-encode/decode batch files for transport
  • Security-tooling deployment scripts that stage .cmd via certutil
  • CI/build agents invoking certutil under cmd.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("MpCmdRun","ccmsetup","choco") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the host — confirm explorer.exe→cmd.exe /c→certutil→cmd.exe /K→powershell.exe and inspect the decoded .cmd content and the PowerShell command line for the staging IP 2.26.252.84. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, kill the powershell/cmd chain, and capture the dropped .cmd and any files written to Temp/Public. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same user's mailbox for the 'Case Documents' lure and check other hosts for certutil -decode + outbound to 2.26.252.84 / 45.158.196.184.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "certutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "decode"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".cmd"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","explorer.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\certutil.exe"
| where CommandLine has "decode" and CommandLine has ".cmd"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 6f2c1a44-7e0b-4d3a-9a6c-2b91e5d8c401

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\certutil.exe OR *\CertUtil.exe OR *\CERTUTIL.EXE) @CommandLine:(*decode*) @CommandLine:(*.cmd*) @ParentImage:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\explorer.exe OR *\EXPLORER.EXE)

| regex("\.cmd", field=CommandLine)
| ParentBaseFileName=/(cmd|explorer)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

HollowFrame staging server download (PowerShell fetch from 2.26.252.84) AIDelivery Medium
Alerts on any endpoint egress to the HollowFrame next-stage staging host 2.26.252.84, or a PowerShell command line referencing that IP. This is the payload-retrieval step after the LNK/certutil chain and uses a hardcoded article IOC. Rationale: 2.26.252.84 is the article's explicitly named PowerShell fetch/staging IP; direct IOC match on any endpoint egress is high-fidelity delivery evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation VMs deliberately contacting the IOC
  • Security researcher lab traffic
  • Proxy/EDR appliance re-checking the indicator
  • Shared NAT gateway where another benign host reused the IP after takedown
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — expect powershell.exe/cmd.exe descended from explorer→certutil chain; confirm on-host payload artifacts. 2) Contain: block 2.26.252.84 at the egress firewall/proxy and isolate any endpoint that connected. 3) Hunt: sweep for the certutil -decode chain (UC1) and any subsequent connections to 45.158.196.184:8888 and github.com/adioziaete/memio.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "2.26.252.84"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "2.26.252.84"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HollowFrame DLL side-load: python.exe loading rogue python311.dll from user-writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the HollowFrame loader's signed-binary side-load pair — legitimate python.exe loading a malicious python311.dll from a non-standard, user-writable directory (Temp, Public, AppData\Roaming, ProgramData) rather than a real Python install root. Rationale: Uses the article's exact side-load pair python.exe + python311.dll and constrains to user-writable directories to separate the HollowFrame drop from real Python installs; corroborated by a public Joe Sandbox python311.dll analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html • https://www.joesandbox.com/analysis/1651022/2/html
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1055
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/embedded Python bundles shipped inside app folders under ProgramData
  • Developer venv or PyInstaller onedir builds unpacked to Temp
  • Data-science tooling running python from a Downloads folder
  • Vendor agents embedding a private Python runtime outside Program Files
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Anaconda3\", @"\miniconda3\", @"\venv\", @"\.venv\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash python311.dll and check reputation/signing; a Rust/Go-linked or unsigned python311.dll next to python.exe in Temp is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the DLL + python.exe copy, and kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: look for the follow-on side-load (version.dll/wtsapi32.dll), scheduled-task persistence, and C2 to 45.158.196.184:8888 or GitHub adioziaete/memio.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "python.exe"
| where FileName =~ "python311.dll"
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Programs\Python", @"\Program Files\Python", @"\Program Files (x86)\Python", @"\WindowsApps\"))
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Downloads\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Matryoshka side-load: version.dll / wtsapi32.dll loaded from outside System32 AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Matryoshka backdoor's side-loaded proxy DLLs — version.dll and wtsapi32.dll — being loaded from any directory outside C:\Windows\System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS. These are genuine Windows library names abused via search-order hijack to run the Rust backdoor. Rationale: version.dll and wtsapi32.dll are the exact Matryoshka side-load DLL names in the article; constraining to loads outside Windows system directories isolates search-order hijack from legitimate OS use. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit third-party apps that ship their own version.dll/wtsapi32.dll in their install directory (common for games/media apps)
  • Portable applications run from USB/Downloads
  • Software installers staging DLLs in Temp before moving to Program Files
  • Developer build outputs containing copied system DLLs
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Downloads\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the DLL's signer and the host process — an unsigned version.dll/wtsapi32.dll in Temp/AppData loaded by a non-OS binary is the Matryoshka indicator; hash and detonate. 2) Contain: isolate the host and quarantine the DLL + its loader. 3) Hunt: correlate with the python311.dll side-load (UC3), scheduled-task persistence, and outbound to 45.158.196.184:8888 or api.github.com for adioziaete/memio.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("version.dll","wtsapi32.dll")
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\", @"\Windows\WinSxS\"))
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Matryoshka HTTP C2 beacon to 45.158.196.184:8888 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on endpoint egress to the Matryoshka backdoor's hardcoded HTTP C2 endpoint 45.158.196.184 on TCP 8888, used by the version.dll variant to spawn a shell and deliver tooling. Uses a fixed IP+port article IOC. Rationale: 45.158.196.184:8888 is the article's explicit Matryoshka HTTP C2 endpoint; a fixed IP+non-standard-port pair is high-confidence C2 evidence with negligible benign traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox/lab detonation of the sample
  • Threat-intel appliance validating the IOC
  • Reuse of the IP by a benign service post-takedown
  • Internal proxy re-checking indicator reputation
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess connecting to 45.158.196.184:8888 — expect a version.dll-hosting signed binary or python.exe; capture the process tree back to the LNK chain. 2) Contain: block the IP at egress, isolate the host, and terminate the beaconing process. 3) Hunt: enumerate AD reconnaissance activity (net/nltest/ldap), scheduled-task persistence, and GitHub C2 to adioziaete/memio on the same and adjacent hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "45.158.196.184" and RemotePort == 8888
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "45.158.196.184" and DstPortNumber == 8888
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Matryoshka GitHub C2: non-browser process polling api.github.com / raw.githubusercontent.com AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Matryoshka wtsapi32.dll variant that uses a private GitHub repo (adioziaete/memio) as C2 — beacon.json/cmd.json/result.json per-host mailboxes. Since traffic is HTTPS, this surfaces unexpected, non-developer processes (python.exe, rundll32, or side-loaded DLL hosts) reaching GitHub API/raw endpoints. Rationale: Article names the private GitHub repo adioziaete/memio and the beacon.json/cmd.json/result.json mailbox structure as C2; HTTPS hides the path, so the detectable pivot is unusual non-dev processes reaching GitHub API/raw hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package managers (pip, npm, go) pulling from raw.githubusercontent.com
  • Update frameworks/agents fetching release assets from GitHub
  • Custom internal automation scripts using the GitHub API
  • Security tooling downloading rule/signature updates from GitHub
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","npm.exe","go.exe","node.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the initiating binary — an unsigned or side-loaded host (python.exe from Temp, or a version.dll/wtsapi32.dll host) polling GitHub on a fixed cadence is the Matryoshka mailbox beacon; check the account adioziaete and repo memio if visible. 2) Contain: block GitHub egress for the offending process/host, isolate the endpoint. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host with the LNK/certutil chain, python311.dll side-load, and 45.158.196.184:8888; review per-host <computer>_<username> directories in the repo history if access is available.
